## RCA COMPLETE — confirmed root cause, and THE OUTAGE IS STILL ACTIVE

First correction to the ticket: it says 'more than 20 minutes'. I verified live just now — `https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/mcp` returns **502 right now, ~4 hours in, with no self-recovery**. Discriminating probe: `/mcp` = 502 while `/review/health` = 200 and `/` = 200, so nginx, Gerrit and the review-bot are all healthy and only the rebar_mcp upstream is dead.

## Confirmed mechanism (on-box, read-only SSM)

1. **The MCP container was OOM-KILLED.** `docker inspect` on `rebar-mcp-8db373933654-8093`: `OOMKilled=true Exit=137 RestartCount=1 Status=exited`, Finished `2026-09-03T01:36:51Z` = **18:36:51 PDT**. The plan-review job started 18:31:33 PDT. **The container died ~3 minutes into the gate run.** Host is a t4g.large, 8 GiB.
2. **nginx still points at the dead port.** `/etc/nginx/mcp-upstream.conf` contains exactly `server 127.0.0.1:8093;` — the port of that exited container. A single backend, no `max_fails`/`fail_timeout`/`backup`/`proxy_next_upstream`, so one dead port is a total outage. Hence 502 rather than a connection refusal.
3. **`restart: always` did not save it** — RestartCount=1 and the container is still `exited`.

## Why it persists — recovery is STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE right now

Redeploy is the only recovery path, and every attempt fails at build:

    error: Required uv version `==0.12.7` does not match the running version `0.12.9`

pyproject.toml:346 pins `required-version = "==0.12.7"` while the Dockerfiles `COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:latest`, which has moved to 0.12.9. Autodeploy is looping on this — fail#3 backoff 240s, fail#4 backoff 480s — so MCP can never rebuild. Filed separately as `febd-6b13-1976-43be` (curbable-regardable-lemming), linked, claimed, and being fixed FIRST since it is the prerequisite.

## A hypothesis I had, correctly REFUTED

I suspected `mcp_mem_abort`/`mcp_retire_cap` — the alarms I had just fixed in bff5. Both are **0.0 in every 900s bucket 15:00-21:45 PDT**, and neither has fired since 2026-08-30. They are DEPLOY-PATH markers, not observers of the serving process, so a KERNEL OOM-kill is invisible to them. Recording this because it is the interesting part: the instrumentation that exists for 'MCP ran out of memory' does not observe the case that actually happened.

## The detection gap (AC(b)) is total

`observability.sh:46-58` probes exactly two endpoints and publishes `gerrit_healthy` and `reviewbot_healthy`. There is **no `mcp_healthy` metric** — confirmed by `list-metrics` on namespace rebar/host. The container's own `/health` is not routed by any nginx location, so it is unreachable from outside the box. The deploy declares success at the flip and never re-validates. So nothing in the system can observe that /mcp is 502.

## Latent defect worth its own attention

In `autodeploy.sh`, `mcp_retire_sweep`'s live-backend guard `[ "$p" = "$live" ] && continue` sits only inside the `Running=true` branch (~line 714). An exited-but-live container falls through to the else branch and is `docker rm`'d while the nginx include still names its port — which is exactly the state observed here. That converts a transient crash into a permanent 502.

## Also noted

Root disk is back to **76% (46G/60G)** and climbing — relevant to `3276-2f81-8c75-4ddd` and epic `6202`, since the 60 GiB grow was explicitly an unwedge, not a fix.

Prior art from the search: `d240-824a-dd04-4cdb` (event-loop block, same nginx-alive/upstream-dead signature), `9d40-1db8-1bcc-4f91` (22min of 502 on the sibling /review service; its fix added a per-container healthcheck), `d80d-7be7-1c0a-4231` (added the very `review_plan_start`/`gate_status` surface in use when this broke).

comments.body:
The `mcp_retire_sweep` reaping defect is FIXED and pushed: Gerrit change 2567 — https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/c/rebar/+/2567 (commit 363e03c8df9c).

## The defect was exactly as diagnosed, confirmed against the code

`infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh`, `mcp_retire_sweep` (function at line 701; the guard was at 714). The live-backend check `[ "$p" = "$live" ] && continue` sat ONLY inside the `Running=true` branch. The `else` arm had **no live check at all** — it reaped any non-running managed container, including the live one.

## The RED proof reproduces this outage's exact signature

Pre-fix, the new test logged:

    {"event":"autodeploy","msg":"mcp retire: reaped exited rebar-mcp-live-8093 (port 8093 freed)"}

That is the observed 2026-09-02 state verbatim — the sweep freeing port 8093 while `/etc/nginx/mcp-upstream.conf` still named `server 127.0.0.1:8093;`. Two tests failed pre-fix (live backend reaped; no signal emitted); the third — a RUNNING live backend — passed before and after as the preserved-behaviour control. Anti-vacuity holds: the same fixture's genuinely superseded exited container on 8092 is asserted reaped in the same run, so the sweep still does its job.

## The fix

The guard is HOISTED above the state branch rather than duplicated into the else arm — a duplicated guard is the same defect waiting to drift, and the code now carries a comment saying so. The `[ -z "$live" ]` fail-safe deliberately stays in the running arm: an exited container on no KNOWN live port is still safe to reap, which an existing test pins.

## A signal was added, on the existing path

An exited container on the live port is not a routine backoff — it means `/mcp` is 502ing right now — so it emits `err mcp-live-backend-down`, an `AUTODEPLOY_ERROR` marker. That reuses the existing convention with ZERO new machinery: `AUTODEPLOY_ERROR` is already counted into `deploy_errors` by observability.sh. A fresh token (as `AUTODEPLOY_MCP_RETIRE_CAP` and `AUTODEPLOY_MCP_MEM_ABORT` are) would have needed its own `publish_autodeploy_marker_delta` call, an offset file, and a terraform metric before it was visible at all. The contrast is deliberate: retire-cap and mem-abort are kept OUT of `deploy_errors` because they are routine; a down live backend is not.

## Verification

`pytest tests/scripts` 1355 passed / 3 skipped; `make lint` exit 0 including shellcheck and all three ratchets. No mechanism marker was needed — a bash marker is not one of the seven censused kinds.

## Noted, not acted on

`autodeploy.sh` is **1313 lines**, far past the 800 cap. It is not gated, because the CI module-size gate scopes to `src/rebar` Python only. Flagging it as a real but out-of-scope observation: the file that manages every deploy on the box is the largest unsplit unit in the tree, and this session has now found two distinct defects in it (this one, and the uv build path).

## Remaining on this ticket

AC(b) detection landed as change 2565 (mcp_healthy probe + alarm — needs a terraform apply to go live). This change addresses the mechanism that made the outage PERMANENT. Still open: AC(a)'s actual OOM prevention — the container was OOM-killed ~3 min into a gate run on an 8 GiB box, and nothing yet stops that recurring. That needs a design decision (container memory limit, gate offloading, or a larger instance) rather than an obvious fix.

comments.body:
## AC(a) research complete — the crux, and why this is EPIC-sized rather than bug-sized

Read-only investigation. Recording before any decision, because the finding changes what AC(a) can honestly mean.

### The crux: gate work runs IN-PROCESS

`src/rebar/_mcp_llm.py:194` — `_spawn_gate_daemon` (function at :157) ends in `threading.Thread(target=_bg, daemon=True).start()`. `review_plan_start` (:255) offloads only the basis-SHA resolution to an anyio worker (:291); the review itself runs as `work=lambda: _review_plan_body(...)` **on that daemon thread inside the uvicorn process**. `offload_sync_tools` (`_mcp_health.py:287`) likewise moves bodies off the event loop but stays in-process. No subprocess, no fork, no worker service.

So the async surface bought TIMEOUT-IMMUNITY, NOT ISOLATION. The gate's memory IS the MCP server's memory. Every other option follows from this.

Two amplifiers, both hardcoded: `plan_review/pass1.py:362,425` runs up to 6 parallel LLM calls and `container_stage.py:44,258` opens a SECOND pool of 6 — each holding prompt plus response. And `PlanContext` (`det_floor.py:141-144`) states the content is "ALWAYS whole (no truncation, no content-chunking, by design)", so for a container ticket every child dict is resident. Ruled out as a cause: the code snapshot streams to DISK, capped at 512 MiB (`workflow/snapshot.py:46,245`) — disk pressure, not RSS.

Second unbounded consumer on the same box: the review-bot calls `rebar.llm` directly in-process (docker-compose.yml:273). Two LLM runtimes on one 8 GiB host.

### Two facts that reframe the problem

1. **There are NO memory limits anywhere** — no `mem_limit`, no `deploy.resources.limits`, on gerrit, review-bot, mcp or opcert. Yet Gerrit IS budgeted (`gerrit.config:48,67`: heapLimit 2g, packedGitLimit 1g, explicitly sized against total box RAM). So ~3 GiB is reserved by design, and the service that RUNS THE GATES is the only one with no budget at all.
2. **Memory is entirely unmetered.** observability.sh publishes gerrit_healthy, reviewbot_healthy, disk_used_percent and root_disk_used_percent — and nothing for memory. `MCP_MEM_MIN_MB=1024` (autodeploy.sh:175) is a one-shot deploy go/no-go that FAILS OPEN, with no derivation from any measurement.

### A documentation-vs-reality mismatch worth its own attention

ADR 0079:88 and ADR 0104:75 both claim the blue-green overlap is "guarded by a memory-pressure alarm". **There is no such alarm.** The only related alarm counts DEPLOY REFUSALS, not memory. That is the same shape of defect as bff5: a stated guard that does not observe the condition it names.

### Prior decisions that constrain the answer

- ADR 0104:75 and ADR 0079:88 **explicitly decided NOT to upsize** — the one-in/one-out overlap cap exists "so the transient 2x rebar-mcp never forces the t4g.large (8 GiB) up to t4g.xlarge". Upsizing contradicts an accepted ADR.
- Ticket 3276's operator-approved principle applies identically: growing a resource is an unwedge, not a fix. An unbounded fan-out will fill 16 GiB too.

### Ranked options

1. **Measure first.** Publish mem_available_percent plus per-container RSS, and a peak-RSS line at gate completion. Prevents nothing on its own — but every other option needs a number nobody has.
2. **Container memory limits on all four services.** Honours the ADR-0104 "fit inside 8 GiB" decision and makes the next failure attributable. Stated plainly: this does NOT save the gate and may kill it sooner. Its value is that MCP can no longer take Gerrit down — and with the reaping fix, `restart: always` and the healthcheck, an MCP OOM becomes a ~30s blip rather than 12 hours.
3. **Bound the in-process footprint** — make the two fan-out widths configurable and lower them, or run the gate as a subprocess so peak RSS is reclaimed on exit. The only structural fix, and real work.
4. **Upsize to t4g.xlarge.** Fastest relief; contradicts two ADRs and the 3276 principle; postpones rather than bounds.

Unnamed until now, and arguably the honest end-state: **move gate execution off the box entirely** (separate instance or Fargate). That dissolves the co-tenancy problem the ADRs are working around, and is bigger than this ticket.

### What is unmeasured — the important finding

Peak MCP RSS during a gate; steady-state RSS per container; how RSS scales with ticket size and fan-out width; actual free memory at the kill. **Any mem_limit or instance size chosen today is a guess**, including the existing 1024 MB deploy floor.

### Recommendation on sizing

AC(a) as written ("prevent the OOM") is a capacity-architecture problem with the same shape as epic 6202 for disk. Proposal, for operator decision: land MEASUREMENT plus CONTAINER LIMITS under this ticket — that, with the two ACs already done, makes the outage observable, attributable and survivable — and decompose in-process gate execution into a sibling epic, mirroring how 3276 spawned 6202. Escalated rather than decided.

## AC(b) IS NOW LIVE — the mcp_healthy alarm is applied and detecting

Operator-approved apply completed. `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms` confirms:

    rebar-mcp-serving-path-down | metric mcp_healthy | Statistic Minimum
    Threshold 1.0 LessThanThreshold | period 300 | EP 3 | DTA 2
    TreatMissingData breaching | 1 alarm action | State INSUFFICIENT_DATA (newly created)

Plan was clean and minimal: **1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy** — this creates a new alarm and touches no existing paging behaviour.

## A false-page risk I checked BEFORE calling this done

The alarm is `treat_missing_data = breaching`, so if the probe that publishes `mcp_healthy` were not yet running on the host, the alarm would have gone to ALARM within ~15 minutes and paged for a non-problem. Verified it will not:

- `get-metric-statistics` returns **22 mcp_healthy datapoints in the last 2 hours** — the metric is publishing.
- The probe is deployed: `grep -c mcp_healthy /opt/rebar/infra/scripts/observability.sh` = 3, file dated Sep 3 07:33.
- `systemctl is-active rebar-observability.timer` = **active**.

So INSUFFICIENT_DATA is simply a newly-created alarm awaiting its first evaluation periods, not a missing publisher.

## What had to be fixed first, and why it matters

Change 2565 landed this alarm with a **1236-raw / 1180-dedented character** `alarm_description` against AWS's 1024 cap, so it was **unappliable** — `terraform plan` errored outright. That reached main through LLM-Review and a green Verified vote because nothing in the pipeline plans against AWS: `terraform validate` parses HCL and passes, the alarm guards checked structure rather than provider constraints, and CI never runs a plan. It surfaced only when an operator asked for the apply.

Change 2584 trimmed the description to 775 characters and added `test_alarm_descriptions_fit_the_aws_limit`, which now covers BOTH the heredoc and quoted-string spellings (monitoring.tf uses the quoted form three times, so a heredoc-only guard would have skipped exactly those) and carries an anti-vacuity floor of 15 measured descriptions. It measures what terraform actually sends — `<<-` strips the common indent, and counting raw would have failed the valid, live `bedrock_invoke_client_errors` at 1037 when AWS reports its description as 982.

## Where this ticket stands

- AC(b) — unhealthy upstream detected and reported: **DONE and LIVE**. Nothing could observe a /mcp outage for the 12 hours of this incident; that gap is now closed in production.
- AC(c) — regression test / operational probe: **DONE** (change 2565's shell tests, RED-proven).
- AC(a) — prevent the OOM: measurement-only instrumentation is in flight per the operator's decision. No memory limit or instance size will be chosen until there are numbers, because today every candidate value is a guess.

Endpoint is healthy: `/mcp` returns 401 (auth required), not 502.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
AC(a) measurement-only instrumentation pushed: Gerrit change 2589 — https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/c/rebar/+/2589 (commit b4fed2147007, 6 files +732/-11). Per the operator's decision: MEASURE FIRST, choose limits later. No mem_limit, no instance-size change, no fan-out change.

## What now publishes, on the existing 5-minute timer, namespace rebar/host

    mem_available_percent          (no dims, Percent)  from `free -k` column 7
    mem_used_percent               (no dims, Percent)  complement
    mem_probe_ok                   (no dims, 1/0)      did the read actually succeed
    container_memory_rss_bytes     (dim: container)    one datapoint per running container
    container_stats_ok             (no dims, 1/0)      the census's own heartbeat

Host gauges are DIMENSIONLESS, matching root_disk_used_percent and every rebar/host alarm in monitoring*.tf — a dimension on one side only silently unmatches. The per-container gauge follows the other local precedent, disk_used_percent's `mount` dimension, because 'which resident set grew' is a comparison ACROSS containers: one `Sum by container` query, versus per-service metric names that would need this probe and every consumer edited whenever compose gains or renames a service.

## Three details that make the measurement trustworthy

1. **It reads `available`, not `free`.** Column 7 of `free -k`, not column 4. On Linux those differ by the reclaimable page cache, and using `free` would have systematically understated headroom — the RED proof for this shows [6] vs [25], so it is not a rounding difference.
2. **`mem_probe_ok` distinguishes a measured zero from a synthesised one.** Both host gauges publish on every tick including failure paths, in each gauge's pessimistic direction (0% available / 100% used) — the same convention section 5's mirror_out_of_sync now uses. But a pessimistic default must never be mistaken for a real reading, so any analysis of this campaign's data must DROP ticks where mem_probe_ok = 0. A genuinely full box publishes a real 0 with mem_probe_ok = 1.
3. **peak_delta_bytes is reported alongside the absolute peak.** `RUSAGE_SELF.ru_maxrss` is a process-wide HIGH-WATER MARK, so in a long-lived MCP server the absolute figure attributes every prior gate run's cost to whichever run you happen to be reading. Without the delta the numbers would be actively misleading for exactly the question being asked.

## Peak RSS per gate run

New `src/rebar/llm/peak_rss.py` emits a `GATE_PEAK_RSS {json}` journald marker at gate completion — gate, ticket_id, peak_rss_bytes, peak_delta_bytes, elapsed_ms, timestamp. A marker rather than metric plumbing because the containers deliberately hold no AWS credentials (IMDS hop limit), which is why VOTER_ERROR and MERGE_CHANGE_ERROR are markers the host probe greps and republishes; the convention is copied verbatim from voter_merge.merge_change_error, including the f829 rule that the logger copy omits the token. It also works under the CLI on a laptop where CloudWatch does not exist.

Seam: the LIBRARY entry points `rebar.llm.review_plan` and `rebar.llm.verify_completion` are wrapped rather than _spawn_gate_daemon and the CLI separately, since both call paths reach the gate through those two functions. Emitted from a `finally`, so runs that DIE — the OOM case, the whole reason this exists — still report.

`ru_maxrss_to_bytes(value, platform)` is a pure function: bytes on darwin/BSD, x1024 on Linux. Kept pure so both branches are testable without the platform.

## docker stats is bounded twice

`--no-stream` plus `timeout 15`, matching the bare `timeout N docker ...` idiom autodeploy.sh already uses in four places. If `timeout` were itself absent the command fails 127, container_stats_ok publishes 0, and the probe continues — it can never wedge the timer. A test asserts both bounds by hanging the stub for 300s unless invoked through timeout AND with --no-stream.

## Eight RED proofs, all binding

publish-nothing-on-failure -> 4 failed ([] != [0]); read `free` not `available` -> 2 failed ([6] != [25]); drop --no-stream -> TimeoutExpired after 60s, the wedge reproduced; gate container_stats_ok on success -> 4 failed; treat ru_maxrss as bytes everywhere -> 3 failed (2048 != 2097152); emit on `else` not `finally` -> 1 failed; logger copy carries the token -> 1 failed (f829 regression); drop the wrapper from review_plan -> 1 failed. All restored, 24/24 green.

## Verification

pytest tests/scripts 1369 passed / 3 skipped; test_gate_peak_rss_9ea3.py 12 passed; make lint exit 0 (mechanism new=0 so NO marker needed, complexity new=0/increased=0); make typecheck 750 files. One caveat carried forward honestly: a full `pytest tests/unit` sweep was started as an extra check and its result was not seen — CI will settle it.

## Next step is DATA, not a decision

Once this lands and deploys, the campaign needs to run long enough to answer: peak MCP RSS during a gate, steady-state RSS per container, and how RSS scales with ticket size. Only then can a mem_limit or an instance size be chosen as anything other than a guess.

comments.body:
Plan-review PASSED and certified (head_sha 31a37c1223411a836edabdea11d87d839264cd74, currency_basis file_impact) after restructuring the plan to the readiness floor. The prior run BLOCKED on two legitimate findings: the ticket was filed with prose bullets rather than a `- [ ]` checklist under `## Acceptance Criteria`, and it named no proving commands — so nothing in it was checkable.

## An acknowledged gap the gate caught, recorded here rather than silently dropped

Advisory T5b/E1: **root cause item 2 — nginx's `upstream rebar_mcp` is a single `server` line with no `max_fails`, `fail_timeout`, `backup` or `proxy_next_upstream` — is named as a confirmed root cause, but no acceptance criterion remediates it and it is not listed among the deliberate exclusions either.** That is accurate and it was my omission: I documented the mechanism and then left it out of the plan in both directions.

Stating the disposition explicitly now. It is **deferred, not fixed**, for these reasons:

- It is a change to the nginx serving TOPOLOGY, not to the capacity question this ticket's remaining scope covers. Adding failover means deciding what the second backend IS — during a blue-green cutover the old container is briefly still alive, but in steady state there is exactly one, so 'fail over to what?' has no answer today without also changing how many MCP backends run.
- With the retire-sweep fix (change 2567, merged) plus `restart: always` and the container healthcheck, a crashed backend is now a ~30s blip rather than permanent. Failover would shrink that further; it is no longer the difference between an outage and no outage.
- The genuine end-state for this — running MCP with more than one backend, or moving gate execution off-box entirely — is the epic-sized work already identified for AC5's data to inform.

I am NOT adding it as an AC to this ticket, because doing so would commit this bug to a topology change the operator has not scoped. Recording it here so it is a decision rather than an oversight, and so the next reader does not have to rediscover that the single-server upstream was known and left.

The other two advisories are non-blocking and noted: AC4 asserts new measurement capability without naming its own novelty explicitly (T3), and a general definition-of-done quality note (P6). Neither changes what the work is.

comments.body:
Change 2589 patch set 2 pushed, addressing all three review findings.

## FINDING 1 (the important one): unbounded metric cardinality

The per-container gauge keyed its CloudWatch dimension on `docker stats {{.Name}}`, and MCP container names embed a per-deploy commit SHA and port. **I have now personally observed THREE distinct MCP container names in this one session** — `rebar-mcp-8db373933654-8093`, `rebar-mcp-3e04025b684e-8092`, `rebar-mcp-81da79273115-8093` — so the growth is measured, not theoretical. Left alone it would bill per unique dimension combination and restart the series at every deploy, making 'peak MCP RSS during a gate' unanswerable. Measurement instrumentation that cannot be charted over time is worse than none, because it looks like coverage.

**Fix:** the dimension key is now `service=` resolved from container LABELS, via a second bounded `timeout 15 docker ps --format ...` joined against the stats stream in one awk pass (`docker stats --format` cannot emit labels, which is why the second call exists). `autodeploy.sh` also stamps `--label rebar.service=mcp` on the blue-green container, and `rebar.service` wins over the compose label so an explicit stamp can override.

**A correction to the implementing agent's stated justification, which I verified against the live box.** It reported that the blue-green MCP container is started by a bare `docker run` that 'compose never sees and never labels', so a label-only read would have left exactly the campaign's container with no identity. That is NOT what the box shows:

    rebar-mcp-81da79273115-8093 :: mcp
    compose-review-bot-1        :: review-bot
    compose-opcert-1            :: opcert
    compose-gerrit-1            :: gerrit

The MCP container DOES carry `com.docker.compose.service=mcp`, inherited from the compose-built image. So a label-only read would have worked today. The explicit stamp is still the better design — it does not depend on image-label inheritance surviving a future image change — but it was a robustness improvement, not the necessity it was described as. Recording this so the commit's reasoning is not taken as verified fact.

Rejected, correctly: parsing `-<sha12>-<port>` off the name. It fails in the DANGEROUS direction — an unmatched name falls through as itself, so a convention change silently restores unbounded cardinality rather than failing loudly. Unlabelled containers go to a single constant `unlabeled` bucket: bounded by construction, obvious in the data, self-healing at the next deploy, with the raw name sent to journald where cardinality is free.

Proven by `test_two_deploys_of_the_same_service_collapse_to_one_dimension_value`, which feeds the two real observed names and asserts `sorted(published) == ['mcp']` while BOTH readings survive under that value — a blue-green cutover briefly runs two containers, and `Maximum by service` is what a peak-RSS question asks. The docker stub is non-vacuous: its `ps` branch exits 3 unless the script actually asked for both label templates. RED: repointing the dimension at the raw name fails 6 of 16.

## FINDING 2: a partial failure looked like success

An unparseable `MemUsage` row was silently dropped while `container_stats_ok` still published 1. ## The OOM arithmetic is now settled — operator supplied the missing term

Operator (2026-09-03): '~10 plan reviews run in parallel frequently.'

2. **The load-side control is the missing lever.** Ten concurrent in-process gates on one 8 GiB host is a capacity decision, not a leak. The options are bounded concurrency (admission control), moving gate execution off-box, or a larger host — and the first two are the ones consistent with this project's stated principle that growing a resource is an unwedge rather than a fix.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
First-hand instance, 2026-09-05 ~10:20 UTC, with the outcome verified rather than assumed — and it is the dangerous shape rather than the benign one.

**What happened.** An MCP `comment_ticket` call exceeded the client's 120s deadline and was moved to a background task. That task then terminated with:

    Task failed: MCP server "rebar" transport dropped mid-call;
    response for tool "comment_ticket" was lost

**What actually happened on the server.** I checked before retrying, and **the write had SUCCEEDED**. The comment is present on the target ticket (`undefiled-revivable-gemsbok`), exactly once. Only the response was lost.

**Why this is worse than a plain timeout.** A lost response on a WRITE is indistinguishable, from the caller's side, from a write that never happened. The obvious recovery — retry — DOUBLE-POSTS. In an append-only event store there is no natural idempotency for a comment: two identical comments are two real events, and nothing later can tell they were one intended write. An agent following normal retry discipline will corrupt the record precisely by being careful.

I avoided it only because I read the ticket back before retrying, which is not a step most callers would think to take on a comment. Worth considering whether write tools should carry a client-supplied idempotency key, or whether the guidance should explicitly say "verify before retrying any MCP write whose response was lost".

**Context, since this bears on the timeout hypothesis.** The call was made while the ticket store was under contention from several concurrent sessions — an earlier `comment_ticket` in the same period also crossed 120s and was backgrounded, but that one returned `{"result": "ok"}` normally. So the slow path here is the store write, not a gate: no LLM operation was running in this session at the time, which argues the 502/drop class is not exclusively tied to long gate jobs as this ticket's title frames it. That is one observation, not a refutation of the gate-job association — but it is a case that does not fit it.

Recording as evidence only; taking no action on this ticket.

## RCA: the MCP RSS growth is NOT a Python object leak — it is per-call peak memory multiplied by unbounded tool concurrency

Investigated under /rebar-debug against a local `rebar-mcp` (Streamable-HTTP, `REBAR_MCP_READONLY=1`) driven with real traffic over a full local clone of this store (8,877 ticket dirs, 255,264 commits).

### What was ruled OUT (with evidence)

1. **Transport / `stateless_http=True`** — 200 sequential `initialize` + `tools/call` round trips: RSS 77.1 MB -> 77.8 MB. Flat. The SDK's stateless path (`mcp/server/streamable_http_manager.py:188-235`) starts a task per request in the lifespan task group; those tasks complete and are released.
2. **Python-level retention on the read path** — `tracemalloc` on the live server across 12 full-store `ready_tickets` calls: traced memory 39.3 MB -> 44.0 MB. Of that +4.7 MB, +2.75 MB is `importlib._bootstrap` (one-time lazy imports). Nothing accumulates.
3. **In-process retention of the compiled store** — 6 sequential `reduce_all_tickets` calls in one process: each holds ~230-257 MB while live, and after `del` + `gc.collect()` traced memory returns to **13.9 MB every time**. Python frees it completely.

### What actually happens (confirmed)

`reduce_all_tickets` (`src/rebar/reducer/_api.py:255-300`) materializes the **complete compiled state of every ticket in the store** into one list. Measured on this store: **243.4 MB** of live Python objects for 8,879 tickets.

Every discovery/graph read reaches it: `list_states` (`src/rebar/_engine_support/reads.py:494`), `find_ready_tickets` (`src/rebar/graph/_ready.py:63`), `search_state` (`reads.py:577`), plus `next_batch`/`deps`/`validate`.

Two multipliers turn that into an OOM:

- **Concurrency.** Every sync MCP tool body is offloaded via `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` (`src/rebar/_mcp_health.py:233-274`) and the default 40-slot limiter is never lowered. Up to 40 full-store compiles can be live simultaneously.
- **The allocator never returns it.** Freed arenas stay mapped, so process RSS is a monotonic high-water mark of the peak concurrency ever reached.

**Measured, on fresh servers, one full-store read per thread:**

| concurrency K | peak RSS | delta over 69 MB base |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 372 MB | +303 MB |
| 2 | 666 MB | +597 MB |
| 4 | 1252 MB | +1183 MB |
| 8 | 2422 MB | +2353 MB |

**RSS = 69 MB + K x 295 MB**, linear, and post-call RSS equals peak RSS in every case — it is never given back. K=16 extrapolates to **4.8 GB**, which is exactly the reported production endpoint (4.5-4.8 GiB). The 40-slot ceiling is ~11.9 GB, far above the 7.6 GiB host — so the process OOMs long before it can plateau, which is why the growth presents as unbounded.

This also explains **load-proportionality** precisely: RSS tracks peak concurrent discovery reads, not elapsed time.

### The specific changeable defect

The lean projection that exists *because* these six fields are 88% of a discovery payload — `LEAN_OMITTED_FIELDS` (`description`, `comments`, `authorship_ledger`, `attestations`, `signature`, `keyring`), `src/rebar/_engine_support/reads.py:426` — is applied **after** the full list is materialized, at `_mcp_reads.py:274` and `reads.py:535`. It reduces wire bytes and does nothing for peak memory: all 8,877 full states are simultaneously live before the first field is dropped.

**Sized directly:** reducing all 8,879 tickets and projecting *inline, per ticket* costs **56.4 MB peak** versus **243.4 MB** today — a **4.3x (77%) reduction**. That moves the K=16 endpoint from ~4.8 GB to ~1.2 GB and the 40-way ceiling from ~11.9 GB to ~2.9 GB, i.e. inside the host.

### Honest characterisation

This is **not a memory leak** — no object graph accumulates and Python reclaims everything. It is an **unbounded peak-memory defect**: growth is bounded in principle, but the bound exceeds host RAM. A container memory limit would therefore be strictly wrong as a fix (it only re-targets the kill); so would a periodic restart. The fix must reduce the per-call peak, which is what the linked change does.

### Not yet tested (residual)

The gate/LLM path was not exercised here. `plan_review/relation_snapshot.py:257` calls `reduce_all_tickets` with all three filters off (the maximal compile) and `PlanReviewGeneration.relation_snapshot` (`plan_review/generation.py:48`) holds it for the whole 15-20 minute review — that is genuine multi-minute retention on top of the same root cause, and overlapping reviews would add to the same curve. It shares the root cause fixed here but its contribution is not separately measured.

Also observed, small and unrelated to the GiBs: `_sha_locks` (`src/rebar/_snapshot/cache.py:58`) grows one `threading.Lock` per distinct SHA with no eviction (~240 B/entry).

### Attribution

`caused_by` -> **98b8-5f08-1569-45cc** ("Make the lean discovery row actually lean", commit `483477df62702`, 2026-08-28), which introduced both late-projection sites. That change measured the 88% figure and correctly applied it at the wire layer, but scoped the projection to the payload and not to the reduction that produces it — a reviewer holding that measurement was in the best position to catch that the full states are still all built first. Recorded as `plan_defect`, not `regression`: peak memory was never better, so no commit "broke" it; the plan simply did not extend to the allocation. Diverges from a whole-file blame majority, which would name the much older `reduce_all_tickets`/`list_states` authorship (`8fdd6ba`/`ad30433`, 2026-06-12) — those lines were correct at the time and predate both the store scale and the MCP concurrency that make them fatal.

## The leak premise is REFUTED. This is load-proportional allocator retention, not a leak.

Recorded here so the next person who sees MCP RSS climb finds the answer instead of re-deriving it. **Do not go looking for an object that accumulates — there isn't one.**

### Proof that nothing is retained

- `tracemalloc` on a live server across 12 whole-store `ready_tickets` calls: traced memory **39.3 MB -> 44.0 MB**. Of that +4.7 MB, +2.75 MB is `importlib._bootstrap` (one-time lazy imports). Traced PEAK in the same window was 288.4 MB.
- Six sequential `reduce_all_tickets` calls in one process: each holds 230-257 MB while live; after `del` + `gc.collect()` traced memory returns to **13.9 MB every single time**.
- Meanwhile RSS rose 464 MB and stayed there.

The retainer is the **allocator** (freed arenas are not returned to the OS), not a Python referrer. That is why every "find the leaking object" search comes up empty.

### The linear model, measured on fresh servers

One whole-store discovery read per thread, K threads, each run on a freshly started server:

| K | predicted `69 + K x 295` | observed peak RSS | observed after |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 364 MB | **372 MB** | 369 MB |
| 2 | 659 MB | **666 MB** | 666 MB |
| 4 | 1249 MB | **1252 MB** | 1250 MB |
| 8 | 2429 MB | **2422 MB** | 2424 MB |

**RSS = 69 MB + K x 295 MB.** `after` equals `peak` in every row — it is never given back. K=16 extrapolates to 4.8 GB, exactly the reported 4.5-4.8 GiB endpoint. The 40-slot `anyio` limiter puts the ceiling at ~11.9 GB against a 7.6 GiB host, so the process OOMs before it can plateau — which is why it presents as unbounded.

This is also why growth is **load-proportional rather than time-proportional**: RSS tracks the peak number of concurrent discovery reads, not elapsed time.

### The defect

`reduce_all_tickets` materializes the complete compiled state of every ticket into one list (243.4 MB for 8,879 tickets). `LEAN_OMITTED_FIELDS` exists precisely because those six fields are ~88% of a discovery payload, but `lean_projection` was applied only AFTER that full list existed (`_mcp_reads.py:274`, `_engine_support/reads.py:535`), so it saved wire bytes and nothing else. Fix: project INSIDE the reduce loop.

### After the fix, same protocol

| K | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 372 MB | **155 MB** |
| 2 | 666 MB | **238 MB** |
| 4 | 1252 MB | **359 MB** |
| 8 | 2422 MB | **740 MB** |

~295 MB -> ~84 MB per concurrent call (3.5x). Ceiling ~11.9 GB -> ~3.4 GB; the observed K=16 workload 4.8 GB -> ~1.4 GB.

### Why the 40-slot limiter was NOT also lowered — do not "fix" this later by lowering it

It is shared by every sync tool, so lowering it queues cheap calls behind whole-store reads that take **16.3 s** each. Measured on the fixed build:

| call | latency |
|---|---|
| `ready_tickets` (whole-store read) | 16.3 s |
| `show_ticket`, server idle | **41.7 s** |
| `show_ticket`, 8 heavy reads in flight | **80.5 s** |

Against the ~60 s MCP client deadline those calls are already at the edge, and a timeout there is the ambiguous signal that provokes duplicate billed gate runs (d80d-7be7-1c0a-4231). Lowering the shared limiter buys a memory ceiling by pushing more calls over that line.

If a fan-out bound is still wanted, the right instrument is a **dedicated limiter on the whole-store compile**, not the shared thread pool. Choosing that width is explicitly deferred on this ticket by operator decision pending AC5 data — the tables above are that data.

### Bearing on AC5

AC5 asked for peak MCP RSS during a gate, steady-state RSS per container, and how RSS scales with store size. The campaign found the governing variable is **concurrency**, not store size or gate phase: 69 MB base, ~295 MB per concurrent whole-store read before the fix and ~84 MB after. Steady state on an idle server is 69 MB; one read takes it to 372 MB and it stays. Whoever closes AC5 should record that "what memory limit / instance size" is answered by **neither — the per-call cost was the defect**.

### Readiness correctness (the lean pass)

`find_ready_tickets` now computes readiness over LEAN states and re-reduces only the ready subset. The byte-identity check covers the `omit_fields=()` default and cannot cover that path, so it is proven separately: readiness reads exactly `ticket_id`, `status`, `parent_id` and `deps` (`relation`/`target_id` via `build_blocked_by`), plus `ticket_type`/`archived` consumed by `reduce_all_tickets`' own filters — none in `LEAN_OMITTED_FIELDS`. `tests/unit/test_ready_lean_equivalence_9ea3.py` proves it by differential execution over a store exercising open/closed/in_progress blockers, both `depends_on` and `blocks` directions, a missing blocker, a non-blocking relation, `epic_filter`, `session_log`/`code_review` artifacts and an event-less debris dir — then repeats it dropping each of the six fields ONE at a time, so a consumed field cannot hide behind the other five. On the real store both passes return the **same 696 ready tickets**, all 696 rehydrated. Seeding `status` into the omit set turns the test red and names it.

### Also found, filed separately

- **`show_ticket` costs 41.7 s idle / 80.5 s under load** — `resolve_ticket_id` falls through to `_scan_alias` (`_ids.py:312`), ~8,900 JSON parses to resolve ONE id. Filed as `lousy-unsuited-gnu` (`94c5-b42e-ac80-4f06`). 9ea3's 502 symptom has TWO independent causes — memory (this change) and latency (that one); fixing this does not fix that.
- **Plan-review retention** — `relation_snapshot.py:257` holds the same whole-store compile for a full 15-20 minute review. Filed as `3499-ee9f-0e1d-443b` (`enduring-ironclad-arrowana`).
- **`_sha_locks`** (`_snapshot/cache.py:58`) grows one `threading.Lock` per distinct SHA with no eviction — genuinely unbounded but ~240 B/entry, not the GiBs.

### Revert condition

If after this deploys MCP RSS still climbs to multiple GiB **while `tracemalloc` shows traced memory flat**, the model is right but the constant is still too large, and the next lever is the dedicated compile limiter or a streaming read — not a hunt for a leaking object. If instead traced memory is seen **growing** in production, this analysis is wrong: there is a retention source the local harness never exercised (most likely the gate/LLM path, which was not driven here), and the investigation should restart there.

## Correction to my own record: tonight's ABSOLUTE latency numbers are confounded by host load

Amending the durable record I posted above, because one class of number in it is weaker than I presented it.

**What is wrong.** I reported `show_ticket` at **41.7 s "on an idle server"**. *Idle* there meant the MCP server had no other in-flight requests — it did **not** mean the host was quiet. That measurement was taken while this box was carrying several concurrent `make verify` runs and multiple agents; load average during my run was ~22-26, and it has since reached 54. So the absolute figure mixes my `_scan_alias` mechanism with ambient contention and **must not be treated as a clean baseline**. The same caveat applies to `ready_tickets` at 16.3 s and `show_ticket` at 80.5 s under 8 heavy reads.

Independently corroborating: `rebar show` calls on this host are currently taking 36-43 s for other operators too, which is the same band — consistent with my number, but exactly why it cannot be attributed to `_scan_alias` alone tonight.

**What survives unchanged.**

1. **The mechanism.** `resolve_ticket_id` falls through to `_scan_alias` (`_ids.py:312`, guard at `:457-460`), which walks every ticket directory and `json.load`s each ticket's CREATE/SNAPSHOT. That is read from the code, not timed, so host load cannot affect it. ~8,900 parses per single-id resolution on this store stands.
2. **The RATIO.** `show_ticket` went 41.7 s -> 80.5 s (**2.0x**) when 8 heavy reads were added, measured back-to-back in the same session under the same ambient load. A ratio between two measurements minutes apart is far more robust to contention than either absolute, and it is the ratio — not the absolute — that carries the argument that the shared limiter already couples cheap and expensive work.
3. **Every memory number.** The K-table, the linear fit, and the before/after are RSS and `tracemalloc` measurements, not latency. They are unaffected by CPU contention: peak RSS for a given K does not change because the host is busy, and each K was measured on a freshly started server. Those stand as reported.

**What this means for the "do not lower the shared limiter" conclusion.** The structural argument is unchanged — the limiter is shared by every sync tool, so lowering it queues cheap calls behind whole-store reads, and the 2.0x coupling is measured. What is *weakened* is the sharper claim that `show_ticket` is "already at the edge of the ~60 s client deadline": if a meaningful part of 41.7 s is ambient load, the quiet-host floor may be materially lower and the margin correspondingly larger. I still would not lower the shared limiter — but that specific deadline-proximity argument should be re-measured on a quiet host before anyone relies on it, rather than quoted from here.

**What to do about it.** The clean split needs an in-process measurement on an unloaded host: count `json.load` calls (or file opens) during a single `resolve_ticket_id`, which is load-independent, and time it separately. That is `lousy-unsuited-gnu` AC2's job and it should be done when this box is quiet. Tonight's absolute latencies belong in that ticket as "observed under load average 22-54", not as a baseline.

I would rather flag this against my own analysis than have someone later find the number does not reproduce on a quiet host and lose confidence in the memory findings, which rest on entirely different and unaffected evidence.

## Observed
On 2026-09-02 the configured rebar MCP endpoint initially accepted tracker calls and started plan-review job 1788399093580353346-ab9badfce4eb4b45a6db70794296455e. A later status poll returned "Transport closed"; every subsequent rebar MCP call returned nginx HTTP 502. The local CLI remained functional.

**Corrected from the original report:** the outage was not "more than 20 minutes". It ran ~18:31 PDT 09-02 to ~06:41 PDT 09-03 — about **12 hours**, with no self-recovery. A human reported it; nothing in the system could observe it.

## Impact
Agents cannot poll gate results, claim work, or perform tracker operations through the required MCP surface. Long gate state is ambiguous and restarting it risks duplicate billed work.

## Root cause (confirmed on-box, read-only)
1. The MCP container was **OOM-killed ~3 minutes into a plan-review gate run** — `docker inspect` reported `OOMKilled=true`, `Exit=137`, finished 18:36:51 PDT against a job started 18:31:33 PDT. Host is a t4g.large (8 GiB) shared with Gerrit, the review-bot and opcert.
2. nginx's `upstream rebar_mcp` is a **single `server` line with no failover**, and still named the dead container's port, so every request 502'd while nginx itself stayed healthy.
3. Recovery was structurally impossible: redeploy is the only path back, and every build failed on `uv required-version ==0.12.7 does not match 0.12.9` (split out as `febd-6b13-1976-43be`, now closed).
4. `mcp_retire_sweep` reaped the exited-but-live container while nginx still pointed at its port, converting a transient crash into a permanent 502.

Ruled OUT: `mcp_mem_abort` and `mcp_retire_cap` both read 0.0 throughout. They are deploy-path markers, not observers of the serving process, so a kernel OOM-kill is invisible to them.

## Reproduction
1. Start an async plan review through MCP.
2. Poll `gate_status` for its job handle.
3. Observe transport closure followed by persistent HTTP 502 responses.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] AC1: an unhealthy MCP upstream is detected and reported with an actionable signal. Verified by `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names rebar-mcp-serving-path-down` showing the alarm live on metric `mcp_healthy`, and by `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace rebar/host --metric-name mcp_healthy` returning datapoints.
- [x] AC2: a regression test covers loss of the MCP upstream. Verified by `python -m pytest tests/scripts/test_observability_mcp_health_9ea3.py -q`, which drives the real `observability.sh` against stubbed 502/timeout responses and asserts a `0` is published rather than nothing.
- [x] AC3: a transient MCP crash can no longer become a permanent 502 via the retire sweep. Verified by `python -m pytest tests/scripts -k retire -q`, including a case that reproduces the incident signature (the sweep freeing the port nginx still names).
- [ ] AC4: host and per-container memory, and peak RSS per gate run, are measured and queryable, so a memory limit or instance size can be chosen from data rather than guessed. Verified by `python -m pytest tests/scripts/test_observability_memory_9ea3.py tests/unit/test_gate_peak_rss_9ea3.py -q`, and post-deploy by `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace rebar/host --metric-name mem_available_percent` returning datapoints and a `GATE_PEAK_RSS` marker appearing in `journalctl` after a gate run.
- [ ] AC5 [non-codebase]: the measurement campaign has produced the numbers the OOM decision needs — peak MCP RSS during a gate, steady-state RSS per container, and how RSS scales with ticket size. Verified by a comment on this ticket recording those figures.

**Deliberately NOT in this ticket, per operator decision:** choosing a container `mem_limit`, an instance size, or a fan-out width. Every candidate value today is a guess; the decision waits on AC5's data. ADRs 0079 and 0104 explicitly decided against upsizing to t4g.xlarge, and `3276`'s operator-approved principle — growing a resource is an unwedge, not a fix — applies identically. Moving gate execution off-box is the honest end-state and is epic-sized.

## Testing

- `python -m pytest tests/scripts/test_observability_mcp_health_9ea3.py -q` — the serving-path probe.
- `python -m pytest tests/scripts/test_observability_memory_9ea3.py tests/unit/test_gate_peak_rss_9ea3.py -q` — the memory instrumentation.
- `python -m pytest tests/scripts -q` — the full shell-probe suite.
